title: Same Raw Model. Different Feedback. Different Behavior.

data.kicker: LLM training cheat sheet · 6 post-training methods
title: Same Raw Model.
Different Feedback.
Different Behavior.

intro.before: Pretraining gives a model knowledge, not manners. Post-training decides

bullets.text: Trains on prompt → ideal response pairs, with loss on the response tokens only
Teaches format, tone and instruction following from demonstrations
Simple, stable and cheap; the first step of nearly every pipeline
Only imitates good answers; it never learns what makes one bad
Humans rank answers, and a reward model learns to predict their choice
PPO maximizes reward minus a KL penalty that keeps it near the reference
The recipe behind InstructGPT and the first ChatGPT
Four models in memory (policy, reference, reward, value) and finicky to tune
Trains directly on chosen vs rejected pairs with a classification-style loss
No reward model and no sampling loop: it’s ordinary supervised training
Stable and cheap; used for open models such as Zephyr and Llama 3
Needs paired preference data and a frozen reference model in memory
Adds an odds-ratio penalty to the SFT loss that favors chosen over rejected
One stage: instruction tuning and preference alignment together
No reference model, so it needs less memory than DPO
Newer (2024), with fewer results at large scale than DPO or RLHF
Needs only a thumbs-up or thumbs-down per answer, not paired comparisons
The loss follows prospect theory: losses weigh more than equal gains
Copes with imbalanced feedback, e.g. many more good examples than bad
A single label carries less signal than a direct A-vs-B comparison
Samples a group of answers per prompt (e.g. 16) and scores each one
Advantage = (reward − group mean) / group std, so no critic model
Shines with checkable rewards (math answers, unit tests), as in DeepSeek-R1
Many samples per prompt, and a flawed reward gets exploited fast

principles.sub: A few thousand clean demonstrations often beat a large noisy set.
No reward model or PPO loop; you only need chosen vs rejected pairs.
Without a reference penalty, the model drifts and exploits reward flaws.

rows.q: Teach format and tone from examples
You have chosen vs rejected pairs
Math or code with checkable answers
Max control, big budget and team

quote.big: You get the behavior you reward.
quote.small: Choose the feedback signal before the algorithm.

1.alt: SFT: for the prompt 'Capital of France?' only the response tokens 'Paris.' carry loss; with p('Paris') = 0.80 the loss is −ln 0.80 = 0.22.

3.alt: DPO: the chosen answer has log-ratio +1.0 and the rejected −1.0; margin 0.1 × 2 = 0.2, loss −ln σ(0.2) = 0.60, with no reward model.
3.svg: <rect x='6' y='8' width='110' height='22' rx='6' fill='#E9F8F4' stroke='#3452C7' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='61.0' y='22.78' font-size='10.5' fill='#1B2440' text-anchor='middle' data-f='sans'>chosen answer</text><text x='126' y='23' font-size='10.5' fill='#3452C7'>log-ratio +1.0</text><rect x='6' y='38' width='110' height='22' rx='6' fill='#FFF1EC' stroke='#D1495B' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='61.0' y='52.78' font-size='10.5' fill='#1B2440' text-anchor='middle' data-f='sans'>rejected answer</text><text x='126' y='53' font-size='10.5' fill='#D1495B'>log-ratio −1.0</text><text x='120' y='80' font-size='10' fill='#43506B' text-anchor='middle'>log-ratio = log π(policy) − log π(ref)</text><text x='120' y='100' font-size='10.5' fill='#1B2440' text-anchor='middle'>margin = 0.1 × (1.0 − (−1.0)) = 0.2</text><text x='120' y='120' font-size='11' fill='#D1495B' text-anchor='middle' data-f='sans'>loss = −ln σ(0.2) = 0.60</text><text x='120' y='142' font-size='10.5' fill='#3452C7' text-anchor='middle'>no reward model, no RL loop</text><text x='120' y='160' font-size='10.5' fill='#43506B' text-anchor='middle'>pushes chosen up, rejected down</text>

4.alt: ORPO: chosen p = 0.6 gives odds 1.5, rejected p = 0.2 gives odds 0.25; odds ratio 6, penalty −ln(6/7) = 0.15, added to the SFT loss.
